    Key Points

    Why Reproducibility Matters

    • Computational reproducibility means someone can take your code, data, and documentation and get the same results
    • There are three levels: numerical reproducibility (same numbers), logical reproducibility (same conclusions), and process reproducibility (same workflow)
    • Reproducibility benefits you first: it’s easier to debug, extend, and share reproducible work

    The Reproducibility Crisis

    • The reproducibility crisis is real, with major consequences for science and careers
    • Common obstacles include environment differences, manual steps, implicit dependencies, and poor documentation
    • A reproducibility checklist helps you identify and close gaps systematically
    • Reproducibility is a practical investment in your research quality and impact

    Project Directory Structure

    • A standard project structure (data/src/results) makes research clear and reproducible
    • Raw data is sacred: keep it original, unchanged, and read-only
    • Processed data should be generated by scripts, not manually edited
    • Results are artifacts that should be regeneratable from code
    • Always use relative paths in code so it’s portable
    • Separating concerns (data, code, results) prevents confusion and accidents

    README and Documentation Files

    • A comprehensive README is essential for reproducibility
    • Document data provenance with source URLs, checksums, and download instructions
    • Processing logs explain how raw data becomes processed data
    • Jupyter notebooks should be exploratory; final analysis belongs in clean scripts
    • A clear project structure section helps newcomers navigate your repository

    Conda Environment Management

    • Your computational environment includes language versions, package versions, system libraries, and OS configuration
    • “It works on my machine” happens when environments differ; reproducibility requires capturing your environment
    • conda is the recommended tool for research; it manages Python packages, R packages, and system dependencies
    • Always export your environment with conda env export and include it in your repository
    • Pin exact versions before publishing for maximum reproducibility

    pip, Docker, and HPC Modules

    • pip and requirements.txt are alternatives for pure Python projects
    • Docker provides maximum reproducibility but adds complexity; useful for complex environments
    • On HPC clusters, document module dependencies separately from conda
    • Apptainer (formerly Singularity) is the Docker equivalent for HPC clusters where Docker is unavailable – on Sagehen: module load apptainer
    • Include environment files, setup scripts, and module lists in your repository

    Introduction to Makefiles

    • Make automates multi-step workflows and only re-runs necessary steps
    • Makefiles explicitly document data dependencies and analysis steps
    • A Makefile target depends on prerequisites; if anything changes, the target is re-run
    • Recipe lines must use TABs, not spaces
    • .PHONY targets like all, clean, and help make your Makefile self-documenting

    Advanced Make Patterns

    • Variables, .PHONY targets, and special variables ($@, $<, $^) make Makefiles clean and maintainable
    • Pattern rules let you define one rule for many similar transformations
    • Make can orchestrate HPC job submissions for parallel processing
    • Debug with make -n (dry run) and make -d (debug output)
    • A good Makefile with help and clean targets makes your workflow self-documenting
    • For complex pipelines with hundreds of jobs, consider Snakemake or Nextflow

    Git for Research Projects

    • Git is valuable for research beyond just code; track analysis decisions, methods, and evolution
    • Use meaningful commit messages documenting why you made changes
    • Avoid tracking: large raw data files, credentials, or binary intermediate results
    • Your git log is a lab notebook showing the progression of your research
    • .gitignore keeps large/sensitive/irrelevant files out of version control

    Branching and Collaboration

    • Branches let you explore different analysis approaches without breaking working code
    • Tag versions for submissions, revisions, and publications
    • Collaborate using shared repositories, feature branches, and pull requests
    • Git history demonstrates reproducibility: others can see exactly what changed and when
    • Don’t track large data, binary files, or sensitive information in Git

    SLURM Pipeline Basics

    • SLURM job dependencies enable reproducible, sequential workflows on HPC
    • Use --dependency=afterok:JOBID to make one job wait for another to complete successfully
    • Job arrays parallelize independent tasks across compute nodes
    • Robust scripts include input verification, error handling, and output verification
    • Debug failed jobs by checking logs, using sacct, and running interactively with salloc

    Multi-Step SLURM Workflows

    • Integrate Make with SLURM for automated, reproducible job submission
    • Track job IDs in files so downstream jobs can declare dependencies
    • Use --dependency=afterok:JID so SLURM enforces ordering between steps
    • Capture environment state, input checksums, and compute metadata for reproducibility
    • Make HPC workflows trackable with clear logging and a make status target
    • Idempotent reruns require both Make’s modification-time tracking and idempotent scripts
    • A complete HPC pipeline includes scripts, src, data, results, and logs directories
    • Verify reproducibility by re-running and diffing outputs; non-zero diff means hidden non-determinism

    Sharing Your Research

    • Choose an appropriate license (MIT for most research code, CC-BY for data)
    • Archive code on Zenodo (or similar) to get a permanent DOI
    • Publish data in appropriate repositories with clear access instructions
    • Use CITATION.cff to specify how your work should be cited
    • Include DOI and reproducibility statements in published papers

    Putting It All Together

    • Comprehensive README is the foundation of research documentation
    • Include overview, quick start, methods, results, and license in your README
    • A reproducibility checklist ensures nothing is missed before publication
    • The complete package includes README, LICENSE, CITATION.cff, environment.yml, and Makefile
    • Checklist before publication ensures your research is discoverable, citable, and reproducible
